title: Python WG (ZAS)
text: 1 Preface

title: Python WG (ZAS)
text:
5.1 venv

Python’s built-in environment manager (like renv in R)
Creates an isolated folder (.venv) inside your project with its own Python interpreter and package library
Nothing installed inside .venv affects other projects or your system Python
Activate it once per terminal session; pip then installs into it automatically

title: Python WG (ZAS)
text:
5.2 pip

Python’s built-in package installer (like install.packages() in R)
Installs from PyPI (the Python Package Index) — analogous to CRAN
Used inside a .venv to keep installs project-local

title: Python WG (ZAS)
text:
5.3 .venv + pip

The modern, lightweight approach: built into Python, no extra installation needed
Workflow:

    python -m venv .venv          # create environment
    source .venv/bin/activate     # activate (Mac/Linux)
    .venv\Scripts\activate        # activate (Windows)
    pip install pandas jupyter    # install packages
    pip freeze > requirements.txt # record dependencies

The .venv folder lives inside your project directory

title: Python WG (ZAS)
text:
5.4 Anaconda

A full Python distribution (~3GB) — heavy, but installed once system-wide
Bundles Python + conda + pip + common scientific packages (numpy, pandas, scipy, etc.)
Managed by the company Anaconda Inc.; conda is their open-source package/environment manager
conda can resolve complex dependency conflicts, including non-Python libraries
Useful if you’re on Windows and have historically had trouble installing scientific packages

title: Python WG (ZAS)
text:
5.5 Comparison to renv

venv (and Anaconda environments) are conceptually similar to using renv in an RProject
The requirements.txt (pip) or environment.yml (conda) is analogous to renv.lock
In Anaconda, (base) = your global package library; any named environment = isolated project library
In R terms: (base) ≈ your system library; a conda/venv environment ≈ an renv project library

title: 2  Getting Set Up
text:
4.1 Why do environments matter?
An environment is an isolated Python installation with its own set of packages. This prevents conflicts between projects that need different versions of the same library.

Project A needs pandas 1.5, Project B needs pandas 2.0 — without environments, one breaks.
Environments make your work reproducible: share environment.yml and anyone can recreate it.

title: 2  Getting Set Up
text:
4.2 Two main approaches









✅ Recommended
Also common




Manager
conda (via Anaconda/Miniconda)
venv (built into Python)


Creates envs with
conda create -n myenv python=3.11
python -m venv myenv


Installs packages
conda install pandas or pip install
pip install pandas


Export env
conda env export > environment.yml
pip freeze > requirements.txt


Best for
Science / data work, manages non-Python deps
Lightweight, web, scripting

title: 2  Getting Set Up
text:
4.3 Anaconda vs Miniconda vs conda

Anaconda — full installer with 250+ pre-installed packages and a GUI navigator. Good default for beginners.
Miniconda — minimal installer, just conda + Python. Faster, leaner, install only what you need.
conda — the command-line tool that ships with both. This is what you actually use.







TipTip



If you are installing fresh: Miniconda is recommended. Anaconda is fine too. Avoid mixing conda and pip installs within the same environment when possible.


Why avoid mixing conda and pip?

conda and pip have separate dependency solvers — they do not communicate with each other.
When you conda install a package, conda carefully balances the whole dependency graph, including non-Python libraries (C, CUDA, etc.).
If you later pip install something in the same environment, pip can silently overwrite or downgrade conda-managed libraries — creating conflicts that are very hard to debug.
Safe rule of thumb: install everything you can via conda (or conda-forge) first. Only fall back to pip for packages not available there.
If you must use pip, always do conda installs first, pip installs last — and never go back to conda install after using pip in that environment.

title: 4  Translate R to Python
text:
5 Assignment operator
You can use <- or = in R.

participant_count <- 12
session_num = 1

But only = in Python.

participant_count = 12
session_num = 1



6 Boolean/logical
All caps in R.

is_recorded <- TRUE
has_video   <- FALSE

Capitalised in Python.

is_recorded = True
has_video   = False



7 Indexing
R: concatenate with c() and indexing begins at 1. Last element with length(x).

scores <- c(72, 85, 61, 90, 78)
first_score <- scores[1]
last_score  <- scores[length(scores)]

Python: concatenate with [] and indexing begins at 1. To extract last element use -1.

scores = [72, 85, 61, 90, 78]
first_score = scores[0]
last_score  = scores[-1]



8 Paste
In R: cat() removes numerical prefix ([1]) added by paste(). New line with \n.

cat(paste("Participant count:", participant_count, "\n"))
cat(paste("Session:", session_num, "\n"))
cat(paste("Mean score:", mean(scores), "\n"))

Python: print() adds new line automatically. f-string handles concatenataion. Using scores.mean() won’t work here because scores is a plain Python list, not a numpy array or pandas series (which it would be if above it was e.g., scores = np.array([72, 85, 61, 90, 78])).

print(f"Participant count: {participant_count}")

Participant count: 12

print(f"Session: {session_num}")

Session: 1

print(f"Participant count: {sum(scores) / len(scores)}")

Participant count: 77.2




9 Function

normalise <- function(x) {
  (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))
}

Python: def to define a function with explictly state what to return

def normalise(x):
    return (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))



10 Arithematic

normalised_scores <- normalise(scores)
cat(paste("Normalised:", normalised_scores, "\n"))

Python: we need to convert to a numpy array first because Python lists don’t support arthimetic operations. This is a huge difference between Python and R. Normally we’d import numpy at the top of the script, but we’ll keep it here for now.

import numpy as np
scores = np.array([72, 85, 61, 90, 78])
normalised_scores = normalise(scores)







TipPython is general-purpose



R was designed from the ground up for statistical computing, so statistical and mathematical operations are baked into the language. Python is a general-purpose programming language not specifically intended for data analysis. Statistical functionality is added through libraries like numpy, pandas, and scipy. That’s why Python is ideal for data processing and R is ideal for analyses.

title: 5  The Stuff You Always Forget
text:
8.1 Lists [ ]
Ordered, mutable, can hold mixed types. The everyday workhorse.
rts = [0.423, 0.381, 0.512, 0.299, 0.478]

rts[0]          # 0.423  — first element (0-indexed!)
rts[-1]         # 0.478  — last element
rts[1:3]        # [0.381, 0.512]  — slice: index 1 up to (not including) 3

rts.append(0.350)          # add one item at the end
rts.extend([0.410, 0.390]) # add multiple items
len(rts)                   # number of items
sorted(rts)                # returns a new sorted list (does not modify rts)
rts.sort()                 # sorts rts in place






NoteR / Matlab



R:      rts <- c(0.423, 0.381, ...)  │  rts[1]  (1-indexed!)
Python: rts = [0.423, 0.381, ...]   │  rts[0]  (0-indexed)
R’s length() → Python’s len()
R’s append() → Python’s .append() or .extend() for multiple items
crumbs: 5  The Stuff You Always Forget

title: 5  The Stuff You Always Forget
text:
8.2 Tuples ( )
Like lists but immutable — contents cannot change after creation. Good for things that should stay fixed (coordinates, column headers, return values from a function).
participant = ('P07', 'Klara', 24)   # id, name, age
participant[0]    # 'P07'
# participant[0] = 'P99'  => TypeError! tuples are immutable

# Unpack a tuple into variables:
pid, name, age = participant
print(name)       # Klara
crumbs: 5  The Stuff You Always Forget

title: 5  The Stuff You Always Forget
text:
8.3 Dictionaries { }
Key–value pairs. Think of named columns, or R’s named lists. Keys must be unique.
trial = {
    'participant': 'P07',
    'condition':   'congruent',
    'rt':          0.423,
    'correct':     True
}

trial['rt']              # 0.423  — access by key
trial['rt'] = 0.399      # update a value
trial['block'] = 1       # add a new key

trial.keys()             # dict_keys(['participant', 'condition', ...])
trial.values()           # dict_values(['P07', 'congruent', ...])
trial.get('block', 0)    # safe access: returns 0 if key missing






NoteR / Matlab



R named list:  trial <- list(participant='P07', rt=0.423)
               trial$rt  or  trial[['rt']]
Python dict:   trial = {'participant': 'P07', 'rt': 0.423}
               trial['rt']








TipTip: When to use which?




List = ordered sequence of similar things
Tuple = fixed record that should not change
Dict = labelled data where you look things up by name

10.4 List comprehensions — compact loops
A Pythonic way to build a new list from an existing one in a single line.
rts_ms = [rt * 1000 for rt in rts]           # convert to milliseconds
fast    = [rt for rt in rts if rt < 0.4]     # filter: keep only fast RTs

Python: rts_ms = [rt * 1000 for rt in rts]
With numpy/pandas, Python is also vectorised. List comprehensions are for plain lists.

title: 5  The Stuff You Always Forget
text:
11.2 Returning multiple values
def rt_stats(times):
    return min(times), max(times), sum(times) / len(times)

lo, hi, avg = rt_stats(rts)   # unpack the returned tuple
print(f'Min: {lo:.3f}  Max: {hi:.3f}  Mean: {avg:.3f}')






NoteR / Matlab



R:      my_fun <- function(x, unit = 's') { ... }
Python: def my_fun(x, unit='s'):  ...
R returns the last expression; Python needs an explicit return.
R returns a list for multiple values; Python returns a tuple (unpack with a, b = fun()).








TipTip



Write a docstring (the triple-quoted string right after def) — it shows up when you call help(my_fun) or hover over it in VS Code.

The release year attribute has varying formats of dates, we need to convert it to a common format(ex. yyyy-mm-dd)
import re
import datetime
from datetime import datetime

#Removes noise from date values and convert to standard datetime strings
def formatDates(messyDate):
    dateStr = messyDate.strip()
    dateStr = re.sub(r'(\d)(st|nd|rd|th)', r'\1', dateStr)
    dateStr = re.sub(' [a-zA-Z]{2} '," ",dateStr)
    pattern = '( -|/)|(-|/ )|( -|/ )'
   
    if re.search(pattern,dateStr):

        dateStr=re.sub(pattern=pattern,string=dateStr,repl="-")
    
    
    dateParsers = ('%Y-%m-%d','%d-%m-%Y','%d-%m-%y','%d %b %Y','%d %b %y','%d %B %Y','%m-%d-%y','%m %d %Y')
    isValidDate = False
    for parser in dateParsers:
        try:
            dateObj = datetime.strptime(dateStr,parser)
#             dateStr = str(dateObj)
            dateStr = dateObj.date()   
            isValidDate = True
        except Exception as e:
            pass
            
    if isValidDate:
        return  str(dateStr)
    else:
        #Dates which dosent lie in the above mentioned date formats(dateParsers) will not be considered
        return None

#This function will find the best match for a country name having errors in their names
def get_most_similar(word,wordlist):
    top_similarity = 0.0
    most_similar_word = word
    for candidate in wordlist:
        similarity = SequenceMatcher(None,word,candidate).ratio()
        if similarity > top_similarity:
                
            top_similarity = similarity
            most_similar_word = candidate
    return most_similar_word

title: 8  Reproducibility and project workflow in Python
text:
8.1 What is reproducibility?
This chapter covers the two layers of reproducibility in Python research projects, then works through the specific tools and conventions that support them. The concepts in sections 1 and 3 apply regardless of programming language; sections 2 and 4 are Python-specific.
Reproducibility means someone else, or future you, can re-run your analysis and get the same result. It operates at two levels:
Environment reproducibility means the same packages and versions are installed. Your code does not break because a collaborator has a different version of pandas.
Workflow reproducibility means the same code runs in the same order and produces the same outputs. No mystery variables, no deleted raw files, no steps that exist only in someone’s memory.
Neither layer is sufficient alone. A perfectly locked environment does not help if the script requires you to run cell 7 before cell 3. Clean, ordered code does not help if it requires a package version nobody can install anymore.
Reproducibility is a spectrum. The goal is not perfection from day one, but deliberate choices that reduce friction for your future self and your collaborators.

WarningCommon failure modes




“It works on my machine” — environment problem
Raw data was overwritten and the analysis cannot be re-run — workflow problem
A notebook gives different results depending on the order cells were run — workflow problem
A script uses an absolute path like /Users/name/projects/... that breaks on every other machine — workflow problem

title: 8  Reproducibility and project workflow in Python
text:
8.2 Virtual environments and file paths

8.2.1 Virtual environments
A virtual environment is an isolated Python installation scoped to a single project. It is the R equivalent of an renv library. The key rule: do not install packages into your global Python.
This working group uses conda. The table below also shows venv + pip as a lighter alternative for pure-Python projects.




Table 8.1







conda (current setup)
venv + pip (alternative)




Create an environment
conda create -n my-env python=3.11
python -m venv .venv


Install packages
conda install pandas or pip install pandas
pip install pandas


Record environment for sharing
conda env export --from-history > environment.yml
pip freeze > requirements.txt


Restore environment
conda env create -f environment.yml
pip install -r requirements.txt


Lockfile (approximately renv.lock)
environment.yml or conda-lock for full pinning
requirements.txt or pyproject.toml + uv.lock


When to use
Non-Python dependencies, HPC clusters, mixed R and Python
Pure-Python projects, lighter setup














Note--from-history vs full export



conda env export pins every package including transitive dependencies and platform-specific build strings, making the file non-portable across operating systems. --from-history records only what you explicitly installed, letting conda resolve the rest per platform. For sharing within a team, --from-history is usually the better choice.


Basic conda workflow:


Terminal

conda create -n zas-pythonistas python=3.11   # create once
conda activate zas-pythonistas                 # activate
conda install pandas matplotlib                # install
conda env export --from-history > environment.yml  # record
conda env create -f environment.yml            # restore (others)







TipPositron



Open the Command Palette and select Python: Select Interpreter, then choose your conda environment. Positron will use it for all terminals and notebooks in the project.








Tipuv: a faster modern alternative



uv is a package and project manager for Python written in Rust, by the team behind the ruff linter. It replaces venv, pip, pip-tools, and pyenv with a single unified tool and is 10 to 100 times faster than pip for installs.
What makes it different from venv + pip:

Generates a proper lockfile (uv.lock) with full dependency graph resolution, a much closer analogue to renv.lock than pip freeze is
Manages Python versions itself: uv python install 3.12, no separate pyenv needed
Scaffolds new projects: uv init my-project
Runs scripts without manual activation: uv run script.py



Terminal

uv init my-project        # scaffold project + pyproject.toml
cd my-project
uv add pandas matplotlib  # install and update lockfile automatically
uv sync                   # restore environment from uv.lock

See: docs.astral.sh/uv




8.2.2 Project-relative file paths
Hardcoded absolute paths break on every machine except the one they were written on. The fix is to construct all paths relative to the project root using pathlib.


Python

from pathlib import Path

# __file__ is the path of the current script
# .parent navigates up one folder at a time
PROJECT_ROOT = Path(__file__).parent.parent

data_path   = PROJECT_ROOT / "data" / "raw" / "stimuli.csv"
output_path = PROJECT_ROOT / "outputs" / "figures"
output_path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create if needed

This is the Python equivalent of here::here() in R. The path resolves correctly regardless of where the script is called from.

title: 8  Reproducibility and project workflow in Python
text:
8.3 Naming conventions and folder structure
These conventions apply in any language. Consistent structure makes projects navigable by collaborators and comprehensible to your future self.

8.3.1 Recommended folder layout


Project structure

my-project/
  data/
    raw/          # original data, never modified
    processed/    # derived data, reproducible from raw
  scripts/        # numbered analysis scripts
  notebooks/      # exploratory .ipynb files
  outputs/
    figures/
    tables/
  docs/           # manuscripts, protocols, notes
  environment.yml # conda environment (or requirements.txt)
  .gitignore
  README.md







ImportantRaw data is sacred



Never overwrite raw data, never modify it in place. All transformations happen in code and produce outputs in data/processed/. If something goes wrong, you can always re-derive processed data from the originals.




8.3.2 File naming




Table 8.2






Rule
Avoid
Prefer




Lowercase only
My Analysis.py
my-analysis.py


No spaces
model results final.csv
model-results-final.csv


Date-prefix versioned outputs
results.csv
2025-05-04_model-results.csv


Verb-first for scripts
data.py
01_clean-data.py


Zero-pad numbered scripts
1_clean.py, 10_model.py
01_clean.py, 10_model.py


Be specific
analysis.py, data2.csv
01_clean-eyetracking.py










8.3.3 README as a map
Every project should answer three questions: what does this project do, how do I run it, and what do the outputs mean?


README.md

# Project name
One sentence describing the study or task.

## Setup
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate zas-pythonistas

## Running the analysis
python scripts/01_clean-data.py
python scripts/02_fit-model.py

## Outputs
outputs/figures/  -- all plots, referenced in the manuscript
outputs/tables/   -- model results tables

title: 8  Reproducibility and project workflow in Python
text:
8.4 Version control with git
Git tracks changes to your files over time so you can see what changed, when, and why, and roll back if something breaks. It is language-agnostic and works for any text-based project. GitHub, GitLab, and Codeberg are hosting platforms for git repositories; git itself runs entirely on your local machine.

8.4.1 Core concepts







Term
What it means




Repository
A folder tracked by git, containing your project and its full history


Commit
A saved snapshot of the project at a point in time, with a message describing what changed


Staging area
A holding zone where you choose exactly which changes to include in the next commit


Branch
A parallel version of the project for developing a feature without affecting the main version





8.4.2 The basic workflow


Terminal

# One-time setup
git config --global user.name  "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

# Start tracking a project
git init                        # initialise a new repo in the current folder

# Day-to-day workflow
git status                      # see what has changed
git add scripts/01_analyse.py   # stage a specific file
git add .                       # stage everything (use carefully)
git commit -m "fix: use relative paths in analysis script"

# Review history
git log --oneline               # compact list of past commits
git diff                        # see unstaged changes line by line



8.4.3 Writing useful commit messages
A good commit message completes the sentence “If applied, this commit will…”. Use a short imperative verb phrase: add, fix, update, remove. Keep it under 72 characters.




Table 8.3






Avoid
Prefer




fixed stuff
fix: use relative paths in analysis script


update
add: conda environment file and README setup instructions


changes
remove: hardcoded absolute paths from all scripts


asdfgh
refactor: split data cleaning into separate script










8.4.4 What to put in .gitignore


.gitignore

# Python
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
*.pyo
.ipynb_checkpoints/

# Conda
.conda/

# Secrets: never commit these
.env
*.key

# Large data files: store elsewhere (e.g. OSF or NAS)
data/raw/
*.csv
*.edf
*.mat



8.4.5 A note on branching
Branches let you work on a new feature or experiment without touching the main version of your project. When the work is ready, you merge it back. For solo projects you may not need branches at all; a clean linear commit history is fine. For collaborative projects, a simple convention is to keep main stable and do all new work on a named branch.


Terminal

git checkout -b feature/add-preprocessing   # create and switch to a new branch
git checkout main                            # switch back to main
git merge feature/add-preprocessing         # merge when ready

Branching and collaborative workflows (pull requests, merge conflicts) will be covered in a future session.

title: 8  Reproducibility and project workflow in Python
text:
8.5 Quarto vs. Jupyter notebooks

8.5.1 They are not competitors
Quarto uses Jupyter as its execution engine. Adding jupyter: python3 to a .qmd header tells Quarto to call Jupyter to run your code. The real choice is between two file formats for your working documents.




Table 8.4







.ipynb notebook
.qmd (Quarto)




File format
.ipynb (JSON)
.qmd (plain text)


Execution order
Any order; cells run independently
Always top to bottom, fresh process


Kernel state
Persists between cells and can be stale
No persistent state between renders


Git diffs
Noisy; outputs embedded in JSON
Clean; plain text only


Output storage
Stored inside the file
Separated from source


Multi-format export
Requires nbconvert and manual steps
Built-in: HTML, Word, PDF, slides


Inline computed values
Not straightforward
`{python} round(val, 2)`


Best for
Exploration, iteration, teaching
Reports, papers, shared outputs










8.5.2 The hidden state problem in notebooks
The biggest reproducibility risk in .ipynb files is out-of-order execution. Jupyter remembers every variable set during a session, even from cells you have deleted or moved. A notebook that appears to work may depend on a variable set hours ago in a cell that no longer exists. The only reliable check is Kernel > Restart & Run All before sharing, and people often forget.


8.5.3 What freeze: true does in Quarto
By default, Quarto re-runs all your code from scratch on every render. This is correct for reproducibility but slow for heavy computations like model fitting or EEG preprocessing. freeze: true changes this behaviour: Quarto caches each chunk’s output and only re-runs a chunk when its source code actually changes.

First render: runs everything and saves outputs into a _freeze/ folder alongside your .qmd
Subsequent renders: skips unchanged chunks and reuses saved outputs
After editing a chunk: only that chunk re-runs

Committing _freeze/ to git means collaborators can render the document and see your outputs without needing your data or compute environment.


_quarto.yml

execute:
  freeze: true







NoteR parallel



freeze: true is roughly analogous to knitr cache = TRUE in R Markdown, but more reliable. It caches at the file level, tracks source changes explicitly, and plays well with git.




8.5.4 A practical two-stage workflow
Use notebooks for the messy exploratory work. Once the approach is settled, move the clean code into a .qmd for the shareable output.


Terminal

# Extract clean code from a notebook when you are ready
jupyter nbconvert --to script exploration.ipynb
# produces exploration.py; paste the useful parts into your .qmd
